== Problem ==
For each positive integer <math>n</math>, let <math>f_1(n)</math> be twice the number of positive integer divisors of <math>n</math>, and for <math>j \ge 2</math>, let <math>f_j(n) = f_1(f_{j-1}(n))</math>. For how many values of <math>n \le 50</math> is <math>f_{50}(n) = 12?</math>

<math>\textbf{(A) }7\qquad\textbf{(B) }8\qquad\textbf{(C) }9\qquad\textbf{(D) }10\qquad\textbf{(E) }11</math>

==Solution 1==
First, we can test values that would make <imath>f(x)=12</imath> true. For this to happen <imath>x</imath> must have <imath>6</imath> divisors, which means its prime factorization is in the form <imath>pq^2</imath> or <imath>p^5</imath>, where <imath>p</imath> and <imath>q</imath> are prime numbers. Listing out values less than <imath>50</imath> which have these prime factorizations, we find <imath>12,18,20,28,44,45,50</imath> for <imath>pq^2</imath>, and just <imath>32</imath> for <imath>p^5</imath>. Here <imath>12</imath> especially catches our eyes, as this means if one of <imath>f_i(n)=12</imath>, each of <imath>f_{i+1}(n), f_{i+2}(n), ...</imath> will all be <imath>12</imath>. This is because <imath>f_{i+1}(n)=f(f_i(n))</imath> (as given in the problem statement), so were <imath>f_i(n)=12</imath>, plugging this in we get <imath>f_{i+1}(n)=f(12)=12</imath>, and thus the pattern repeats. Hence, as long as for a <imath>i</imath>, such that <imath>i\leq 50</imath> and <imath>f_{i}(n)=12</imath>, <imath>f_{50}(n)=12</imath> must be true, which also immediately makes all our previously listed numbers, where <imath>f_1(x)=12</imath>, possible values of <imath>n</imath>.

We also know that if <imath>f_1(x)</imath> were to be any of these numbers, <imath>x</imath> would satisfy <imath>f_{50}(n)</imath> as well. Looking through each of the possibilities aside from <imath>12</imath>, we see that <imath>f_1(x)</imath> could only possibly be equal to <imath>20</imath> and <imath>18</imath>, and still have <imath>x</imath> less than or equal to <imath>50</imath>. This is because if <imath>f_1(x)=20</imath> or <imath>18</imath>, <imath>f_2 (x) = 12</imath>. This would mean <imath>x</imath> must have <imath>10</imath>, or <imath>9</imath> divisors, and testing out, we see that <imath>x</imath> will then be of the form <imath>p^4q</imath>, or <imath>p^2q^2</imath>. The only two values less than or equal to <imath>50</imath> would be <imath>48</imath> and <imath>36</imath> respectively. From here there are no more possible values, so tallying our possibilities we count <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(D) }10}</imath> values (Namely <imath>12,18,20,28,32,36,44,45,48,50</imath>).

~Ericsz, reworded and minor edits by monkey_land

== Solution 2 (''Rigorous'' reasoning on why there cannot be any other solutions) ==
First, take note that the maximum possible value of <imath>f_1(n)</imath> for <imath>1 \le n \le k</imath> increases as <imath>k</imath> increases. When we increase <imath>k</imath>, we either include a new value of <imath>n</imath> that has more divisors than any previous values of <imath>n</imath>, increasing the maximum of <imath>f_1(x)</imath>, or none of the new <imath>n</imath> have more divisors, which would leave the maximum of <imath>f_1(x)</imath> the same as before. In other words, <imath>f_1(x)</imath> is increasing. This means that <imath>f_1(x)</imath> decreases when we decrease <imath>k</imath>. 

Also, let <imath>f_1(n) = 2d(n)</imath> where <imath>d(n)</imath> is the number of divisors of n.

Since <imath>n \le 50</imath>, <imath>f_1(n) \le 20</imath>. This maximum occurs when <imath>d(n) = 10 \implies n = 2^4 \cdot 3 = 48</imath>. Next, since <imath>f_1(n) \le 20</imath>, <imath>f_1(f_1(n)) \le 12 \implies f_2(n) \le 12</imath>. This maximum occurs when <imath>d(f_1(n)) = 6 \implies n = 2 \cdot 3^2 = 18, n = 2^2 \cdot 3 = 12</imath>. Since <imath>f_2(n) \le 12</imath>, <imath>f_1(f_2(n)) \le 12 \implies f_3(n) \le 12</imath>, once again. This maximum again occurs when <imath>d(f_2(n)) = 6 \implies f_2(n) = 2^2 \cdot 3 = 12</imath>. Notice that, from this point on, for <imath>k \geq 3 </imath>, <imath>f_k(n) \leq 12</imath> by a straightforward induction argument.

On a hunch, we investigate what happens when <imath>f_2(n) < 12</imath>, as this is the first time when <imath>f_k(n)</imath> is bounded to a maximum of 12.
Suppose for the sake of contradiction that <imath>f_2(n) < 12</imath>. Then, <imath>f_3(n) < 12</imath>, as <imath>f_2(n) = 12</imath> is the only number that would maximize <imath>f_3(n))</imath> for <imath>f_2(n) \le 12</imath>. As a result, since <imath>f_1(n)</imath> is increasing, and because <imath>12</imath> is the only value for which <imath>f_1</imath>  is maximized, <imath>f_1</imath> "steps down" from a maximum of <imath>6 \cdot 2 = 12</imath> if <imath>n < 12</imath>. This means we must have that <imath>f_1(f_3(n)) < f_1(12) = 12 \implies f_4(n) < 12</imath>. We continue applying <imath>f_1</imath> on both sides (which is possible since <imath>f_1</imath> is increasing) until we reach <imath>f_{50}</imath>, giving us that <imath>f_{50}(n) < 12</imath>. However, <imath>f_{50}(n) = 12</imath>, which is a contradiction. Thus, <imath>f_2(n) = 12</imath>. 

Now, we can finally solve for the solutions with a clean conscience - we proceed similarly to Solution 1. <imath>f_2(n) = 12 \implies f_1(f_1(n)) = 12 \implies d(f_1(n)) = 6</imath>. <imath>d(f_1(n)) = 6</imath>. This gives us two cases. First, we have the case where <imath>f_1(n) = p^2 \cdot q</imath> where <imath>p</imath> and <imath>q</imath> are primes. Second, we have the case where <imath>f_1(n)=p^5</imath> where <imath>p</imath> is a prime.  For both cases, since <imath>f_1(n) \le 20</imath>, <imath>f_1(n)</imath> can only be <imath>12</imath>, <imath>18</imath>, or <imath>20</imath>.

If <imath>f_1(n) = 12</imath>, then <imath>d(n) = 6 \implies n = p^5, p^2 \cdot q \implies n \in \{ 12, 18, 20, 28, 32, 44, 45, 50 \}</imath>, resulting in 8 solutions. 

If <imath>f_1(n) = 18</imath>, then <imath>d(n) = 9 \implies n = p^8, p^2 \cdot q^2 \implies n = 36</imath>, giving us one more solution. Finally, <imath>f_1(n) = 20 \implies d(n) = 10 \implies n = p^9, p^4 \cdot q \implies n = 48</imath>. 

Thus, in total, we have <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(D)} 10}</imath> solutions.

== Solution 3 == 
<math>\textbf{Observation 1}</math>: <math>f_1 \left( 12 \right) = 12</math>.

Hence, if <math>n</math> has the property that <math>f_j \left( n \right) = 12</math> for some <math>j</math>, then <math>f_k \left( n \right) = 12</math> for all <math>k > j</math>.

<math>\textbf{Observation 2}</math>: <math>f_1 \left( 8 \right) = 8</math>.

Hence, if <math>n</math> has the property that <math>f_j \left( n \right) = 8</math> for some <math>j</math>, then <math>f_k \left( n \right) = 8</math> for all <math>k > j</math>.

<math>\textbf{Case 1}</math>: <math>n = 1</math>.

We have <math>f_1 \left( n \right) = 2</math>, <math>f_2 \left( n \right) = f_1 \left( 2 \right) = 4</math>, <math>f_3 \left( n \right) = f_1 \left( 4 \right) = 6</math>, <math>f_4 \left( n \right) = f_1 \left( 6 \right) = 8</math>. Hence, Observation 2 implies <math>f_{50} \left( n \right) = 8</math>.

<math>\textbf{Case 2}</math>: <math>n</math> is prime.

We have <math>f_1 \left( n \right) = 4</math>, <math>f_2 \left( n \right) = f_1 \left( 4 \right) = 6</math>, <math>f_3 \left( n \right) = f_1 \left( 6 \right) = 8</math>. Hence, Observation 2 implies <math>f_{50} \left( n \right) = 8</math>.

<math>\textbf{Case 3}</math>: The prime factorization of <math>n</math> takes the form <math>p_1^2</math>.

We have <math>f_1 \left( n \right) = 6</math>, <math>f_2 \left( n \right) = f_1 \left( 6 \right) = 8</math>. Hence, Observation 2 implies <math>f_{50} \left( n \right) = 8</math>.

<math>\textbf{Case 4}</math>: The prime factorization of <math>n</math> takes the form <math>p_1^3</math>.

We have <math>f_1 \left( n \right) = 8</math>. Hence, Observation 2 implies <math>f_{50} \left( n \right) = 8</math>.

<math>\textbf{Case 5}</math>: The prime factorization of <math>n</math> takes the form <math>p_1^4</math>.

We have <math>f_1 \left( n \right) = 10</math>, <math>f_2 \left( n \right) = f_1 \left( 10 \right) = 8</math>. Hence, Observation 2 implies <math>f_{50} \left( n \right) = 8</math>.

<math>\textbf{Case 6}</math>: The prime factorization of <math>n</math> takes the form <math>p_1^5</math>.

We have <math>f_1 \left( n \right) = 12</math>. Hence, Observation 1 implies <math>f_{50} \left( n \right) = 12</math>.

In this case the only <math>n</math> is <math>2^5 = 32</math>.

<math>\textbf{Case 7}</math>: The prime factorization of <math>n</math> takes the form <math>p_1 p_2</math>.

We have <math>f_1 \left( n \right) = 8</math>. Hence, Observation 2 implies <math>f_{50} \left( n \right) = 8</math>.

<math>\textbf{Case 8}</math>: The prime factorization of <math>n</math> takes the form <math>p_1 p_2^2</math>.

We have <math>f_1 \left( n \right) = 12</math>. Hence, Observation 1 implies <math>f_{50} \left( n \right) = 12</math>.

In this case, all <math>n</math> are <math>12, 18, 20, 28, 44, 45,</math> and <math>50</math>.

<math>\textbf{Case 9}</math>: The prime factorization of <math>n</math> takes the form <math>p_1 p_2^3</math>.

We have <math>f_1 \left( n \right) = 16</math>, <math>f_2 \left( n \right) = f_1 \left( 16 \right) = 10</math>, <math>f_3 \left( n \right) = f_1 \left( 10 \right) = 8</math>. Hence, Observation 2 implies <math>f_{50} \left( n \right) = 8</math>.

<math>\textbf{Case 10}</math>: The prime factorization of <math>n</math> takes the form <math>p_1 p_2^4</math>.

We have <math>f_1 \left( n \right) = 20</math>, <math>f_2 \left( n \right) = f_1 \left( 20 \right) = 12</math>. Hence, Observation 1 implies <math>f_{50} \left( n \right) = 12</math>.

In this case, the only <math>n</math> is <math>48</math>.

<math>\textbf{Case 11}</math>: The prime factorization of <math>n</math> takes the form <math>p_1^2 p_2^2</math>.

We have <math>f_1 \left( n \right) = 18</math>, <math>f_2 \left( n \right) = f_1 \left( 18 \right) = 12</math>. Hence, Observation 1 implies <math>f_{50} \left( n \right) = 12</math>.

In this case, the only <math>n</math> is <math>36</math>.

<math>\textbf{Case 12}</math>: The prime factorization of <math>n</math> takes the form <math>p_1 p_2 p_3</math>.

We have <math>f_1 \left( n \right) = 16</math>, <math>f_2 \left( n \right) = f_1 \left( 16 \right) = 10</math>, <math>f_3 \left( n \right) = f_2 \left( 10 \right) = 8</math>. Hence, Observation 2 implies <math>f_{50} \left( n \right) = 8</math>.

Putting all cases together, the number of feasible <math>n \leq 50</math> is <math>\boxed{\textbf{(D) }10}</math>.
